title: Erdős #1014 OQ-04: R(4,l+1)/R(4,l) → 1 via Mattheus–Verstraëte
description: Resolves the k = 4 case of Erdős Problem #1014: R(4,l+1)/R(4,l) → 1 as l → ∞. OQ-01 settled k = 3 with the Kim–Shearer quadratic lower bound; this entry settles k = 4 using the 2024 Mattheus–Verstraëte determination of the order of magnitude of the off-diagonal Ramsey number R(4,l) = Θ(l³/(log l)⁴). The proof mirrors OQ-01 one dimension up: the Ramsey recurrence gives the increment R(4,l+1) − R(4,l) ≤ R(3,l+1), which grows like l² (via the AKS upper bound R(3,l) = O(l²/log l)), while R(4,l) itself grows like l³ (the Mattheus–Verstraëte lower bound). Hence R(4,l+1)/R(4,l) − 1 ≤ (4C/c)·(log l)⁴/l → 0. The two deep bounds are stated as axioms (published theorems); the Ramsey-number infrastructure (definition, recurrence, monotonicity, positivity) is inherited from OQ-01.

meta.author: Erdős
meta.assumptions: Two assumptions, both literal `axiom` declarations in Erdos1014OQ04.lean, each a published theorem stated as a hypothesis: (1) `R3_upper_bound_aks` — the Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi (1980) upper bound R(3,l) ≤ C·l²/log l for large l; (2) `R4_lower_bound_mv` — the Mattheus–Verstraëte (2024) lower bound R(4,l) ≥ c·l³/(log l)⁴ for large l. The inherited Ramsey-number infrastructure adds no assumption: `ramseyNumber` (imported from Erdos1014OQ01.lean, defined via `Nat.find`) rests on `ramsey_theorem`, which is fully proved by strong induction in RamseysTheorem.lean (no sorry, no axiom in its dependency chain), so `ramseyNumber` and its recurrence/monotonicity/positivity are axiom-free. The `multicolor_ramsey_exists` axiom in RamseysTheorem.lean is declared after `ramsey_theorem` and is not in this file's dependency chain. The unrelated Kim–Shearer axiom `R3_lower_bound` in Erdos1014OQ01.lean is NOT used by this file either. Accordingly both `meta.axiomCount` and `leanFile.axiomCount` are 2, counting exactly the two literal `axiom` declarations in this file. 0 sorries. The analysis lemmas ((log l)⁴/l → 0, the increment bound) and the main convergence proof are otherwise axiom-free, resting only on Mathlib and the foundational axioms.

crossReferences.description: Answers the k = 4 case of Erdős #1014: does R(k,l+1)/R(k,l) → 1? OQ-04 is the k = 4 analogue of the parent's k = 3 resolution.
OQ-01 resolved k = 3 (R(3,l+1)/R(3,l) → 1) using the Kim–Shearer lower bound and supplied the Ramsey-number definition, recurrence, monotonicity, and positivity that OQ-04 reuses one dimension up.

OQ-02 quantifies the *rate* of convergence for k = 3 as O(log l / l). OQ-04 establishes convergence for k = 4; its increment/denominator gap (l² vs l³) gives a rate O((log l)⁴/l), the k = 4 counterpart of OQ-02's analysis.

sections.title: Imports and the Two Deep-Result Axioms
sections.summary: Imports Mathlib and Proofs.Erdos1014OQ01 (Ramsey-number definition and its proved properties). Opens Real, Filter, Topology, Asymptotics. Declares the two published-theorem axioms: R3_upper_bound_aks (AKS 1980: R(3,l) ≤ C·l²/log l for large l) and R4_lower_bound_mv (Mattheus–Verstraëte 2024: R(4,l) ≥ c·l³/(log l)⁴ for large l).
sections.mathContext: The two axioms are the only new assumptions of this file. All Ramsey-number infrastructure (definition, recurrence, monotonicity, positivity) is inherited from OQ-01; the Kim–Shearer R3_lower_bound of OQ-01 is not used here.

sections.title: Step 1: Increment Bound from the Ramsey Recurrence
sections.summary: increment_bound_k4: R(4,l+1) ≤ R(4,l) + R(3,l+1) for l ≥ 1, the k = 4 specialisation of OQ-01's general Ramsey recurrence (ramsey_recurrence 4 l). The increment R(4,l+1) − R(4,l) is thus controlled by R(3,l+1), one Ramsey dimension below.
sections.mathContext: $R(4,l+1) - R(4,l) \le R(3,l+1)$: the growth of $R(4,\cdot)$ between consecutive arguments is bounded by a $k=3$ Ramsey number, which grows only like $l^2$.

sections.title: Step 2: (log l)⁴/l → 0
sections.summary: Three private lemmas establishing the decay driving the whole argument. rpow_quarter_pow_four: (x^{1/4})⁴ = x for x ≥ 0. tendsto_log_pow_four_div_atTop: (log x)⁴/x → 0, from log x = o(x^{1/4}) (isLittleO_log_rpow_atTop) raised to the 4th power (.pow) then .tendsto_div_nhds_zero, congr'd through rpow_quarter_pow_four. eventually_log4_div_small: for every ε > 0, eventually (log l)⁴/l < ε over natural l, by composing with tendsto_natCast_atTop_atTop.
sections.mathContext: $(\log x)^4 = o(x)$ because $\log x = o(x^{1/4})$; the polylog factor $(\log l)^4$ is negligible against the linear factor $l$, which is exactly the gap between the $l^3$ denominator and the $l^2$ increment.

sections.title: Main Theorem: R(4,l+1)/R(4,l) → 1
sections.summary: erdos_1014_k4_ratio_convergence: for every ε > 0, eventually |R(4,l+1)/R(4,l) − 1| < ε. Extracts constants C, c from the two axioms and a threshold from eventually_log4_div_small(ε·c/(4C)). Positivity (ramsey_pos) and monotonicity (ramsey_monotone_right) give |R'/R − 1| = (R' − R)/R with R > 0. A calc chains: (R' − R)/R ≤ R(3,l+1)/R (increment) ≤ 4C·l²/R (AKS, dropping the log and absorbing the +1 via ((l+1)² ≤ 4l²) ≤ 4C·l²/(c·l³/(log l)⁴) (MV) = (4C/c)·(log l)⁴/l < ε.
sections.mathContext: $\dfrac{R(4,l+1)}{R(4,l)} - 1 \le \dfrac{R(3,l+1)}{R(4,l)} \le \dfrac{4C\,l^2}{c\,l^3/(\log l)^4} = \dfrac{4C}{c}\cdot\dfrac{(\log l)^4}{l} \to 0$: the cubic denominator dominates the quadratic increment, forcing the ratio to 1.

overview.historicalContext: Erdős Problem #1014 asks whether consecutive off-diagonal Ramsey numbers satisfy R(k,l+1)/R(k,l) → 1 as l → ∞ for fixed k ≥ 3 — i.e. whether the Ramsey sequence grows smoothly with no anomalous jumps relative to its size. OQ-01 resolved k = 3 using Jeong Han Kim's 1995 lower bound R(3,l) ≥ c·l²/log l (matching the Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi 1980 upper bound), giving R(3,l) = Θ(l²/log l). The k = 4 case remained out of reach until 2024, when Sam Mattheus and Jacques Verstraëte determined the order of magnitude of R(4,l), proving R(4,l) = Θ(l³/(log l)⁴) — a landmark that resolved a long-standing question on off-diagonal Ramsey growth (published in the Annals of Mathematics). This entry leverages that breakthrough: with the order of magnitude of R(4,l) now known, the same recurrence-plus-growth argument that settled k = 3 goes through one dimension up, resolving k = 4.
overview.problemStatement: Does R(4,l+1)/R(4,l) → 1 as l → ∞? (The k = 4 case of Erdős #1014.)
overview.text: Yes. The Ramsey recurrence bounds the increment R(4,l+1) − R(4,l) by R(3,l+1) ~ l², while the Mattheus–Verstraëte theorem gives R(4,l) ~ l³. The cubic denominator dominates the quadratic increment, so R(4,l+1)/R(4,l) − 1 ≤ (4C/c)·(log l)⁴/l → 0.
overview.proofStrategy: Combine the k = 4 Ramsey recurrence (increment ≤ R(3,l+1)) with the AKS upper bound on R(3,·) (numerator ~ l²) and the Mattheus–Verstraëte lower bound on R(4,·) (denominator ~ l³). The ratio minus 1 is then bounded by (4C/c)·(log l)⁴/l, which tends to 0 because (log l)⁴ = o(l). The polylog factors in both bounds are irrelevant to convergence — any bounds of order l² (numerator) and l³ (denominator) suffice.
keyInsights: The argument is dimension-agnostic in structure: OQ-01 (k = 3) divided a linear increment (~ l) by a quadratic-over-log value (~ l²/log l); OQ-04 (k = 4) divides a quadratic increment (~ l²) by a cubic-over-polylog value (~ l³/(log l)⁴). In both cases the increment is one Ramsey dimension below the value, so the ratio → 1.

The 2024 Mattheus–Verstraëte determination of R(4,l) = Θ(l³/(log l)⁴) is exactly the input that unlocks k = 4: before it, no lower bound of the right cubic order was available, so the denominator could not be shown to dominate the increment.

The polylog factors ((log l)⁴ in the MV bound, the 1/log l in AKS) do not affect convergence — only the polynomial orders l² and l³ matter. The proof isolates this by absorbing every log into the single decay lemma (log l)⁴/l → 0.

The increment bound R(4,l+1) − R(4,l) ≤ R(3,l+1) is a pure consequence of the general Ramsey recurrence proved axiom-free in OQ-01 — the two published-theorem axioms enter only as the growth-rate inputs, keeping the recurrence machinery honest.

Honest axiom accounting: the only assumptions are the two deep bounds stated as `axiom` declarations (published theorems beyond Mathlib's current reach) — so meta.axiomCount = leanFile.axiomCount = 2. The inherited Ramsey-number infrastructure adds nothing: `ramseyNumber` rests on the fully proved `ramsey_theorem`, not on the later `multicolor_ramsey_exists` axiom, so it is axiom-free.
prerequisites: Off-diagonal Ramsey theory and the growth of R(3,l), R(4,l)

conclusion.summary: Resolves the k = 4 case of Erdős #1014: R(4,l+1)/R(4,l) → 1 as l → ∞. The Ramsey recurrence bounds the increment R(4,l+1) − R(4,l) by R(3,l+1) ~ l² (AKS upper bound), while the 2024 Mattheus–Verstraëte theorem gives R(4,l) ~ l³. The cubic denominator dominates the quadratic increment, so the ratio minus 1 is bounded by (4C/c)·(log l)⁴/l → 0. Two published-theorem axioms, and the inherited Ramsey-number infrastructure is axiom-free (meta.axiomCount = leanFile.axiomCount = 2); 0 sorries.
conclusion.implications: Extends the ratio-convergence resolution of Erdős #1014 from k = 3 to k = 4, immediately on the back of the Mattheus–Verstraëte breakthrough. The proof isolates the general mechanism — increment one Ramsey dimension below the value — so that any future determination of the order of magnitude of R(k,l) for k ≥ 5 would let the same argument settle that case too. The decay lemma (log l)⁴/l → 0 and the recurrence specialisation are reusable for higher k.
openQuestions: The general k ≥ 5 case: R(k,l+1)/R(k,l) → 1 would follow from the same argument given a lower bound of the correct order l^{k-1}/polylog on R(k,l), which is not yet known for k ≥ 5.
The rate of convergence for k = 4: the proof gives O((log l)⁴/l), the k = 4 analogue of OQ-02's O(log l / l) for k = 3 — is it tight?
An unconditional (axiom-free) formalization awaiting a Lean/Mathlib proof of the AKS and Mattheus–Verstraëte bounds, which would upgrade this entry from axiomatized to verified.

mainTheorems.description: The k = 4 case of Erdős #1014: R(4,l+1)/R(4,l) → 1 as l → ∞. Proved from the Ramsey recurrence plus the AKS upper bound on R(3,·) and the Mattheus–Verstraëte lower bound on R(4,·).

mainTheorems.name: increment_bound_k4
mainTheorems.description: The k = 4 Ramsey recurrence increment bound R(4,l+1) ≤ R(4,l) + R(3,l+1), specialising OQ-01's general recurrence.

mainTheorems.description: The decay lemma (log x)⁴/x → 0, from log x = o(x^{1/4}) raised to the 4th power. Isolates the polylog factors so only the polynomial orders l², l³ drive convergence.

mainTheorems.name: R3_upper_bound_aks
mainTheorems.description: Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi (1980), stated as a hypothesis: R(3,l) ≤ C·l²/log l for large l. Supplies the ~l² numerator bound.
mainTheorems.leanType: ∃ C > 0, ∃ L₀, ∀ l > L₀, (ramseyNumber 3 l : ℝ) ≤ C * l² / Real.log l

mainTheorems.description: Mattheus–Verstraëte (2024), stated as a hypothesis: R(4,l) ≥ c·l³/(log l)⁴ for large l. Supplies the ~l³ denominator bound.
mainTheorems.leanType: ∃ c > 0, ∃ L₀, ∀ l > L₀, (ramseyNumber 4 l : ℝ) ≥ c * l³ / (Real.log l)⁴
